preamble: Solve the clues and fit the solutions in the diagram jigsaw-wise, wherever they will go.

clue.text: Like the RAs in A, no ruddy use holding informal talks — you just get mews

parts.note: the RAs (Royal Academicians) are artists, and the answer at 8 across puts artists 'in crime', so this phrase supplies the last word

indicators.note: to use something is to work it, and worked material gets rearranged into a new order
holding means gripping from both sides, so the jumbled letters close around another piece

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be jumbled
chats are casual conversations

explanation.surface: A grumble that idle chatter among Academicians is useless: all you hear is cats.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue leans on 8 across, ARTISTS IN CRIME: RAs are artists, so what they are 'in' is the outer word. Cri du chat is French for 'cry of the cat'.
explanation.definitionFit: The genetic syndrome is named after the high-pitched, kitten-like crying of affected babies, so a mewing sound is its hallmark.

clue.text: See 1 across
Among two books concluded game, I'm told

indicators.note: something among others is surrounded by them, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: two in Roman numerals, split to hold the books
the New Testament, the usual crossword books
a chess game ends when the king is mated

explanation.surface: Someone passes on a rumour that a game has finished between two volumes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm told' reads as hearsay, which is the sense of something merely intimated; in chess a game is concluded when the king is mated.
explanation.definitionFit: To intimate is to hint or make known indirectly, a quieter way of saying something was communicated.

clue.text: Surprise has one distressed, knocked over too

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an unexpected result, as when an underdog wins
third meaning: tipped onto its side

explanation.walkthrough: Three separate meanings of one word, strung together with filler that makes it read like one shocking event.
explanation.definitionFit: The word serves as a noun for a shock result, an adjective for emotional disturbance and a past participle for toppling something.

clue.text: "Bonjour" 'll be Spooner's slur on type of Brit

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner famously slurred words by swapping their opening sounds

parts.note: swap the opening B and J sounds of the French greeting with its contracted 'will'

explanation.surface: A sneer that the Frenchman's greeting is a dig at the typical Englishman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bonjour'll' said aloud is roughly BON-JOOR-L; swapping B and J gives JON-BOOL. The blogger who solved it thought the swap a stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: John Bull is the stout cartoon personification of England, a stock figure for the stereotypical Englishman.

clue.text: Ackland has cane and perfume comes from it

parts.note: Joss Ackland was an English stage and film actor
a cane is a walking stick

explanation.surface: An actor carries a walking cane, and scent wafts from it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surname leads to the first name of the actor, a British stage and screen veteran.
explanation.definitionFit: Joss sticks are incense sticks, burned to release fragrant smoke into a room.

clue.text: The helping part, complete with C (for cold)

parts.note: surface: the bit of the body that lends help, as in a helping limb
setter's reading: the answer is read as two letter-and-word chunks which, finished off with C, form the familiar hot-and-cold marking on taps

explanation.surface: A riddle about which body part helps, with a hint about a letter for chilliness.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as 'H and', the answer waits for C to make 'H and C', the hot and cold labels on British taps.
explanation.definitionFit: Lending a hand is giving help, so this body part stands for assistance in the familiar idiom.

clue.text: Casks with which playwright's entertained some cooks

indicators.note: a host who entertains takes guests in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: J. M. Barrie, Scottish author of Peter Pan, with the possessive S

indicators.note: some of a thing is only a portion, so just the opening letters are kept

parts.note: only some of the word is wanted: its first two letters, a selection rather than an abbreviation

explanation.surface: A dramatist offers a few chefs barrels of drink at his house.
explanation.walkthrough: CO inside BARRIE'S. The blogger disliked 'some' for just two letters, but it is a recurring convention for a word's opening.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrico is a small keg or water cask, an old seafaring word borrowed from Spanish.

clue.text: This answer, if you're sharp, you will have guessed

definitions.text: This answer, if you're sharp, you will have guessed

parts.note: surface: if you are quick-witted, the solution should come easily
setter's reading: sharp means sour-tasting, and the old catchphrase says the answer is a certain sour citrus fruit

explanation.surface: The setter teases that any clever solver will already know this one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The answer's a lemon' is a dismissive British phrase meaning there is no good answer; a lemon is also sharp in flavour.
explanation.definitionFit: The citrus fruit is the byword for a sharp, sour taste, and features in the stock retort about answers.

clue.text: Marsh work (sic) — train time's right — makes classy crooks

indicators.note: to make is to construct, so the letters are built into something new

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written without the apostrophe
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A note on a work about wetlands, with a railway timetable aside, turned into a tale of stylish villains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marsh' is Ngaio Marsh, the New Zealand detective novelist, not a bog; Artists in Crime is one of her Inspector Alleyn novels. The bracketed 'sic' looks editorial but is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The title names a Ngaio Marsh novel, and taken literally it describes skilled, stylish criminals.

clue.text: Conduct ungreen in key in English lake

indicators.note: one thing in another is enclosed by it, so a piece is placed inside a larger one

parts.note: Wast Water is the deepest lake in England, in the Lake District
taken as written
G is a musical key

explanation.surface: Environmentally careless behaviour in a musical key, set by an English lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English lake' tempts you to look for a lake as the answer; it only supplies the outer letters, and the answer is the behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: Squandering a precious resource like this is the kind of environmentally careless behaviour campaigners condemn.

clue.text: Half time is money — thus do Hebrews think

parts.note: the prefix for half
T is the abbreviation for time
taken as written
M is short for money, as in the economists' M1

explanation.surface: A play on 'time is money', offered as a stereotype about Jewish thinking.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes the proverb; the cryptic reading cuts it into letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A Semitism is a way of thinking or turn of phrase characteristic of Semitic peoples, such as a Hebrew idiom.

clue.text: Girl to girl turning where the river's blue

parts.note: Vi, short for Violet

indicators.note: turning round faces the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a girl's name

explanation.surface: One girl turns to another by the banks of a blue river.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition alludes to Strauss's waltz The Blue Danube; the Danube flows through the Austrian capital.
explanation.definitionFit: The Austrian capital stands on the Danube, the river celebrated in the famous Strauss waltz as blue.

clue.text: Talking (when M?), I grant, with net perplexed

indicators.note: a perplexed mind is muddled, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone concedes a point in a chatty argument while puzzled by a net.
explanation.walkthrough: The aside '(when M?)' is a joke: with M for the first letter the answer would become MATTERING, talk that matters.
explanation.definitionFit: Nattering is a British colloquial word for chatting idly at length, so it fits talking.

clue.text: Exciting! Poor George, topped, wants common sense

indicators.note: topping something cuts off its head, so the opening letter goes
poor means in bad shape, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: the name without its first letter
nous is British slang for practical good sense

explanation.surface: Poor George has been beheaded and lacks gumption, which is exciting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topped' is a gruesome joke on beheading, and here it only takes the G. The blogger first wrote EGREGIOUS, which fits neither the wordplay nor 'Exciting'.
explanation.definitionFit: Erogenous zones are areas of the body sensitive to sexual arousal, hence stimulating in that sense.

clue.text: Dealer in death, starter to one for tape

parts.note: a race starter fires a pistol
an athlete heads for the finishing tape

explanation.surface: A sinister trader in death, plus something about the start of a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' looks like a first letter, but it means the starting gun of a race.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who smuggles weapons illegally trades in instruments of killing, a grim but fair description.

clue.text: Return to holding and the rest is set

indicators.note: returning means going back the way you came, so the letters are read backwards
holding something means gripping it, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: taken as written, split to hold the next piece
etc. is short for et cetera, and the rest

explanation.surface: An instruction to go back, holding on, while everything else is fixed in place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' looks like a verb of coming home, but it tells you to read the built-up piece backwards. 'Set' is a loose definition: an octet is a particular sort of set.
explanation.definitionFit: An octet is a group of eight, whether musicians or items, so it counts as one kind of set.

clue.text: Bite's proof: sound horn! Harm caused by final drink

parts.note: a toot is the sound a horn makes

indicators.note: something caused is brought about, read loosely as letters worked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be jumbled

indicators.note: the final part of a word is its end, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A warning about a bite: hoot the horn, since a last drink caused harm.
explanation.walkthrough: The blogger thought 'caused' an unjustifiable anagram signal; it is the weakest link in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The impression teeth leave in skin or food is the physical evidence that something was bitten.

clue.text: Here cowboys were to Shanks's mare confined?

definitions.text: Here cowboys were to Shanks's mare confined?

parts.note: surface: a place where cowboys perform, riding broncos
setter's reading: walking everywhere means riding no horse at all, so the cowboys rode zero

explanation.surface: A wry picture of cowboys forced to walk because they had no horses.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it RODE O: rode nothing. Shanks's mare (or pony) is a British idiom for your own legs, travelling on foot.
explanation.definitionFit: A rodeo is a public show of cowboy skills like bronco riding and roping, the natural setting for cowboys.

clue.text: St Vincent's city: like one like him, dressed

parts.note: kin are relatives, alike in family
dressed means wearing clothing, so a garment wraps the next piece
Vincent was a saint, so one like him is a St

explanation.surface: A city named for a saint is described as like one of his kind, clothed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Him' points back to St Vincent in the definition, so the second 'like' gives a saint; 'dressed' both supplies the garment and puts the saint inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingstown is the capital of St Vincent and the Grenadines, the Caribbean island nation named after the saint.

clue.text: Many provided with provisions, vexed

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, a crossword 'many'
provided that means if
given food

explanation.surface: Crowds given supplies are still annoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Provided' and 'provisions' look like the same idea twice; one is a conjunction, the other means food.
explanation.definitionFit: Miffed is an informal word for mildly annoyed or put out, close in meaning to irritated.

clue.text: Brother to Bartle, governor of the Cape

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the French word for a male sibling, also used for a friar
second meaning: surname of the Victorian colonial administrator Sir Bartle, who governed Cape Colony

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a family tree; really it is a French word and a historical surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Frère means brother in French, and Sir Bartle Frere was the nineteenth-century British governor of Cape Colony.

clue.text: Last wish with "status _" gives Mastermind

indicators.note: something that gives yields under pressure and changes shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the last letter of the alphabet
taken as written
the missing word in the Latin phrase status quo

explanation.surface: A dying wish, together with keeping things as they are, produces a criminal genius.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last wish' looks like a phrase, but 'Last' is Z on its own. Mastermind is a long-running BBC quiz programme with a famous black chair.
explanation.definitionFit: Mastermind is a specific British television programme of the general-knowledge contest type, so it is an example of the category.

clue.text: Last first, with little beast to fasten tight

parts.note: the last letter of the alphabet
I as a figure 1, first
a young dog

explanation.surface: An odd order that the last comes first, with a small animal to tie down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last first' looks like a reordering instruction; it is two separate letters, the end of the alphabet and the number one.
explanation.definitionFit: Closing a garment with its zip fastener secures it snugly, which is what fastening tight describes.

clue.text: I'm only here for beer — so NIMBY ends

parts.note: NIMBY stands for Not In My Back Yard, so the phrase ends in this word

explanation.surface: A drinker's excuse for turning up, set against a protester's slogan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm only here for the beer' was a Double Diamond advertising slogan; the clue gives no signal to read the last word backwards, which solvers must infer.
explanation.definitionFit: A dray is a low cart traditionally used by brewers to deliver barrels, so it exists purely to carry beer.

clue.text: Next port with annals shows it may not take

indicators.note: a show is a performance, so the letters put on a new display in a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Historical records of the next harbour reveal something that might not succeed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take' is used in the medical sense: a graft that takes is accepted by the body.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving an organ from one species into another often triggers rejection, so the graft may fail to establish.

clue.text: Conformist customers (as always) right

parts.note: an old word for you, the paper's readers and so its customers
taken as written
aye is a poetic word for ever
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper's motto that the customer is always right, made into a description of a conformist.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes 'the customer is always right'. Customers as YE is a stretch: the setter is addressing the solvers who buy the paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who habitually agrees with authority rather than challenging it goes along with the crowd.

clue.text: Beside traditional fire a chance to bet

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the iron rod kept by an open hearth for stirring coals
second meaning: a card game played for stakes

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a cosy fireside gamble; the two halves are separate senses of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names both a metal rod for stirring a coal fire and a card game where players wager.
